clinicalPearls: A chronic degenerative deposition of calcium in the fibrous ring supporting the mitral valve, most often affecting the posterior annulus
Behaves as a marker of the same risk profile as atherosclerosis, being commoner with advancing age, hypertension, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease with disordered calcium-phosphate handling
Usually an incidental echocardiographic or chest radiograph finding, but extensive calcification can cause functional mitral regurgitation or, less often, mitral stenosis
Associated with an excess of atrial fibrillation, conduction disturbance when calcium encroaches on the atrioventricular node, and systemic embolism
Occasionally the calcified mass liquefies centrally (caseous MAC), which can be mistaken for a tumour or abscess on imaging
Extensive annular calcium complicates surgical and transcatheter mitral intervention and raises procedural risk
Management is directed at the underlying vascular risk factors and any consequent valve dysfunction or arrhythmia rather than the calcium itself
reference.pathophysiology: Mitral annular calcification is a degenerative process in which calcium and phosphate are deposited within the fibrous annulus of the mitral valve, sharing mechanisms with atherosclerosis and with the disordered mineral metabolism of chronic kidney disease. The rigid, calcified ring loses its normal systolic contraction and can prevent adequate leaflet coaptation, producing regurgitation, while heavy calcium extending onto the leaflet bases narrows the inflow and mimics rheumatic mitral stenosis. Encroachment of calcium on the conduction tissue near the atrioventricular node underlies the associated bradyarrhythmias, and the calcified surface may act as a nidus for thrombus or, rarely, infection.
additionalDifferentials: Degenerative aortic valve calcification with annular extension
Cardiac tumour or thrombus (caseous MAC mimic)
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic echocardiography to localise the calcification and quantify any stenosis or regurgitation
Transoesophageal echocardiography for clearer annular and leaflet detail and to exclude endocarditis
Cardiac CT to characterise the extent and distribution of calcium and clarify a caseous mass
Cardiac MRI to distinguish caseous calcification from tumour or thrombus
Assessment of renal function and calcium-phosphate balance and of cardiovascular risk factors
redFlags: Haemodynamically significant mitral stenosis or regurgitation causing heart failure
High-grade atrioventricular block from calcium involving the conduction system
Systemic embolism or stroke arising from the calcified valve
A mobile mass or new regurgitation with fever suggesting superimposed endocarditis
reference.prognosis: The calcification itself is usually benign and slowly progressive, but its presence signals a heightened cardiovascular and mortality risk, and extensive disease can produce valve dysfunction, conduction block, and difficult mitral intervention.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing caseous mitral annular calcification as a tumour or abscess and pursuing unnecessary surgery
Overlooking conduction disease when calcium extends towards the atrioventricular node
Attributing all mitral stenosis to rheumatic disease and missing heavy annular calcium
Underestimating the added risk that annular calcium brings to mitral valve surgery or transcatheter repair
references: Braunwald's Heart Disease: A Textbook of Cardiovascular Medicine
ESC/EACTS Guidelines for the management of valvular heart disease
